overview: Eric V of Denmark was Danish king whose reign involved noble constraints and ended in a famous murder. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1259 — Becomes king as a child; 1282 — Royal charter limits power; 1286 — Murdered.
He died in 1286, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Eric V of Denmark was born c. 1249. His family background is usually placed in House of Estridsen, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Eric V of Denmark's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Eric V of Denmark, called Klipping, is remembered above all through a famous constitutional concession and a famous murder. Pressed by a powerful and resentful nobility, he was forced in 1282 to grant a charter — often called Denmark's first — that bound the king to summon assemblies and respect law, a humiliation for royal authority that reflects a reign of weakness against the magnates.

His death sealed his notoriety: he was killed in 1286, stabbed many times in a barn at Finderup, in one of the most sensational political murders of the Scandinavian Middle Ages. Suspicion fell on leading nobles, and the unsolved killing became a lasting subject of ballad and tradition.

The sources convey a king who could not master his aristocracy and who met a violent end, but they preserve little of his individual temperament. He survives as a figure of royal weakness and dramatic murder rather than as a rounded personality, his reign remembered for the charter forced upon him and the assassination that ended it.

contentSections.title: As king of Denmark
paragraphs: Eric V came to the throne as a child under his mother’s regency. His reign saw aristocratic pressure and the issuing of a royal charter that limited arbitrary royal action.
As King of Denmark, Eric V of Denmark had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Murdered at Finderup in 1286, one of medieval Denmark’s most famous political killings.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Eric’s reign is remembered for the struggle between monarchy and magnates.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Eric V of Denmark's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.
